ai.literal: Those of evil deeds do not fear; noble people fear the delusion called evil deed.
ai.translation: Those who habitually commit evil do not fear it, but noble people dread the delusion of committing an evil deed.
ai.modern: தீய செயல்களைச் செய்பவர்கள் அதற்கு அஞ்சமாட்டார்கள்; ஆனால் மேன்மையானவர்கள் தீவினை என்று சொல்லப்படும் செருக்கிற்கு (மன மயக்கத்திற்கு) அஞ்சுவார்கள்.
ai.explanation: This couplet contrasts how different people view harmful actions. Those who are already accustomed to doing wrong do not fear the consequences of their actions. In contrast, noble and virtuous people dread even the arrogant delusion ('cerukku') that makes one think they can commit an evil deed and escape its effects. The poet uses 'cerukku' to highlight that committing evil stems from a false sense of pride and mental blindness, which the wise carefully avoid.

ai.literal: Because evil deeds yield evil results, evil deeds must be feared even more than fire.
ai.translation: Since evil deeds produce only evil consequences, one must dread committing evil even more than fire.
ai.modern: தீய செயல்கள் தீமையான விளைவுகளையே தருவதால், தீய செயல்களை நெருப்பை விடவும் அதிகமாக அஞ்ச வேண்டும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet warns us about the severe consequences of committing evil deeds. The poet compares the danger of evil actions to fire, which is universally feared for its destructive power. While fire can burn a person physically, its damage is immediate and visible. In contrast, evil deeds yield bad consequences that follow a person relentlessly, destroying their inner character and future. Therefore, one must dread committing evil even more than they fear physical fire.

words.gloss: even to those who harm us

ai.literal: Among all knowledge, the foremost they say is, evil deeds, even to those who harm us, without doing, refraining.
ai.translation: They say the supreme wisdom among all forms of knowledge is to refrain from doing evil, even to those who cause us harm.
ai.modern: அறிவுகள் எல்லாவற்றிலும் முதன்மையானது என்று அறிஞர்கள் கூறுவது, நமக்குத் தீங்கு செய்பவர்களுக்கும் நாம் திரும்பத் தீமை செய்யாமல் தவிர்ப்பதே ஆகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet defines the highest peak of human wisdom. While there are many forms of worldly knowledge, the foremost (தலை) is the moral strength to refrain (விடல்) from doing evil deeds (தீய செய்யா). Crucially, this restraint must be maintained even toward those who actively hate or harm us (செறுவார்க்கும்). True wisdom is not merely intellectual; it is the practical, ethical choice to break the cycle of retaliation.

ai.literal: Even forgetting, another's ruin do not plot; if plotted, virtue will plot the plotter's ruin.
ai.translation: Do not plot another's ruin, even through forgetfulness; if you do, Virtue itself will plot your ruin.
ai.modern: மறந்தும் கூடப் பிறருக்குக் கேடு செய்ய நினைக்கக் கூடாது; அப்படி நினைத்தால், நினைத்தவனுடைய அழிவை அறமே நினைத்துச் செய்யும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet warns against harboring thoughts of doing harm to others, even in a moment of forgetfulness or inattention. The key word 'சூழற்க' (do not plot) emphasizes that even the mental act of planning harm is dangerous. If one violates this and plots harm ('சூழின்'), 'அறம்' (Virtue or the moral law of the universe) will actively plot ('சூழம்') the ruin ('கேடு') of that plotter ('சூழ்ந்தவன்'). This personification of Virtue as an active agent that retaliates against evil thoughts highlights the inescapable nature of moral consequences.

ai.literal: Thinking 'I am a poor man', do not do evil deeds; if done, a poor man he will become again once more.
ai.translation: Do not commit evil deeds thinking, 'I am poor.' If you do, you will only become poorer once again.
ai.modern: நான் ஏழை என்று நினைத்துத் தீய செயல்களைச் செய்யக் கூடாது; அவ்வாறு செய்தால், மீண்டும் மேலும் வறுமை உடையவன் ஆகிவிடுவான்.
ai.explanation: This couplet warns against using poverty as an excuse to commit wrongful or evil deeds. A person might think that because they have nothing, they are justified in resorting to bad deeds to survive. However, the poet warns that doing evil to escape poverty will only result in falling into even deeper poverty and ruin in the future. The words 'மற்றும்' and 'பெயர்த்து' emphasize the repetitive and compounding nature of this downfall, showing that evil actions inevitably multiply one's misery rather than relieving it.

ai.literal: Deeds of an evil nature, oneself towards others should not do, if consequences of a painful nature, oneself afflicting, he does not desire.
ai.translation: A person who does not wish for painful sufferings to afflict themselves should never commit deeds of an evil nature against others.
ai.modern: தன்மீது துன்பங்கள் வந்து சேர்வதை விரும்பாத ஒருவன், பிறருக்குத் தீமையான செயல்களைச் செய்யக் கூடாது.
ai.explanation: This couplet establishes a direct causal link between the harm we do to others and the suffering we experience ourselves. The word 'தீப்பால' refers to actions that belong to the category of evil, while 'நோய்ப்பால' refers to the painful consequences that naturally follow such actions. The poet advises that if a person wishes to remain free from affliction ('அடல் வேண்டாதான்'), the only sure way is to refrain from doing evil to others ('பிறர்கண் செய்யற்க'). It teaches that avoiding harm to others is ultimately an act of self-preservation.

ai.literal: Whatever enmity incurred-those-even will-escape; evil-deed-enmity without-ceasing behind going will-destroy.
ai.translation: Those who have incurred even the greatest of enmities may still escape and survive; but the enmity of one's own evil deeds will relentlessly follow and destroy them.
ai.modern: எத்தகைய பகையை அடைந்தவர்களும் தப்பிப் பிழைத்துக் கொள்ள முடியும்; ஆனால் தீய செயல்களால் வரும் பகையானது அழியாமல் பின் தொடர்ந்து சென்று அழித்துவிடும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the inescapable nature of the consequences of evil deeds. A person might manage to survive or escape even the most powerful external enemies they have angered. However, the enmity generated by one's own bad actions (vinaippakai) is different; it does not fade away or perish. It relentlessly pursues the wrongdoer, following them wherever they go, and ultimately brings about their destruction.

ai.literal: The ruin of those who did evil deeds is like [their] shadow staying at [their] feet without leaving.
ai.translation: The ruin of those who commit evil deeds will pursue and destroy them, just as one's own shadow stays at one's feet and never leaves.
ai.modern: தீய செயல்களைச் செய்தவர்கள் அழிவது, அவர்களுடைய நிழல் அவர்களை விட்டு நீங்காமல் அவர்களுடைய காலடியிலேயே தங்கியிருப்பதைப் போன்றது ஆகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet warns that escape from the consequences of evil deeds is impossible. Just as a person's shadow is inseparable from them and stays right at their feet ('அடி', written here as 'அஇ') wherever they go, ruin ('கெடுதல்') will inevitably follow and catch up with those who do evil ('தீயவை செய்தார்'). The metaphor of the shadow ('நிழல்') emphasizes that retribution is not an external force but an inherent, inescapable consequence of one's own actions.

ai.literal: If one is indeed a lover of oneself, let one not approach the side of evil deeds, even in the slightest measure.
ai.translation: If a person truly loves themselves, let them not approach the path of evil deeds, even in the slightest degree.
ai.modern: ஒருவன் தன்னைத்தானே நேசிப்பவனாக இருந்தால், எவ்வளவும் சிறியதான தீய செயல்களின் பக்கமும் அவன் நெருங்காமல் இருக்க வேண்டும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet explains that true self-love lies in protecting oneself from harm, which can only be achieved by avoiding bad deeds. The word 'kātalaṉ' refers to one who loves, here meaning someone who desires their own true well-being. If a person has this genuine love for themselves, they must not commit any 'tīviṉai' (evil deed), even a tiny fraction ('eṉaittu oṉṟum'). Avoiding the path of evil is presented as the ultimate act of self-preservation, as evil deeds inevitably bring ruin to the doer.

words.gloss: one who is free from ruin

ai.literal: One who is free from ruin, that, let it be known, if he does not do evil deeds by straying into deviant paths.
ai.translation: Know that a person is secure from ruin if they do not stray into deviant paths to commit evil deeds.
ai.modern: ஒருவன் நெறிதவறிச் சென்று தீய செயல்களைச் செய்யமாட்டான் என்றால், அவன் அழிவில்லாதவன் என்பதை அறிந்து கொள்க.
ai.explanation: This couplet explains how one can remain secure from personal downfall. The key word 'அருங்கேடன்' refers to a person whose ruin is extremely rare or impossible, meaning they are indestructible. The poet states that this security is guaranteed if ('எனின்') a person does not stray ('மருங்கோடி') into wrong paths to commit harmful actions ('தீவினை செய்யான்'). Here, 'மருங்கு' literally means 'side' or 'slope', representing a deviation from the straight path of virtue. Thus, avoiding harmful actions is the ultimate shield against ruin.
